Electromagnetic compatibility · Signal integrity · Transmission lines

When PCB Traces Become Transmission Lines: Crosstalk, Reflections and EMC

From a 10 m coupled-cable experiment to PCB-level signal-integrity and radiated-emission simulations.

Digital circuits can fail even when their logical design is correct. Fast voltage transitions propagate as electromagnetic waves, reflect at impedance discontinuities and couple into nearby conductors. This laboratory project combined oscilloscope measurements on a ribbon cable with PCB transmission-line simulations to investigate practical electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) techniques.

10 mExperimental cable length
45 nsMeasured one-way delay
62.8 ΩSimulated series termination

Measuring propagation on a real cable

The first setup used a three-conductor, 10 m ribbon cable. A pulse was injected into one conductor and observed at the far end. By adjusting the load, the report obtained an approximately matched condition at 253 Ω. The observed one-way delay was 45 ns.

Transmission-line fundamentals
v = ℓ / tp
Z0 = √(L′ / C′)   and   v = 1 / √(L′C′)

Here, ℓ is cable length, tp is one-way propagation time, and L′ and C′ are inductance and capacitance per unit length. Using the measured values:

v = 10 / (45 × 10−9) ≈ 2.22 × 108 m/s
L′ = Z0/v ≈ 1.14 μH/m
C′ = 1/(Z0v) ≈ 17.8 pF/m

The propagation speed is approximately 74% of the speed of light. The extracted quantities describe the distributed line, not a single lumped inductor or capacitor.

Grounding the two adjacent ribbon conductors changed the measured matching resistance to approximately 152 Ω. The cable geometry and return-current environment therefore materially changed the line's electrical properties.

Near-end and far-end crosstalk

Next, the team drove one conductor and measured the voltage induced on a neighboring conductor. Near-end crosstalk (NEXT) is observed at the source end of the victim line; far-end crosstalk (FEXT) is observed at the opposite end. The two mechanisms reflect capacitive and inductive coupling between conductors.

The report measured a near-end disturbance of approximately 2.355 V in one configuration. Increasing the input rise time broadened the observed pulse and, at sufficiently slow transitions, reduced its peak amplitude.

With a grounded conductor positioned between the driven and observed conductors, the measured near-end amplitude decreased to about 0.840 V. This demonstrates the influence of conductor placement and a grounded return path on coupling in the tested geometry.

The far-end experiment produced a measured disturbance of approximately −1.19 V, with a reported input rise time of 26.2 ns. Slowing the transition reduced the peak disturbance in the observed case.

Why edge speed matters
fedge ≈ 0.35 / tr

For a single-pole response, this approximation relates the 10–90% rise time tr to bandwidth. Faster edges contain more high-frequency energy, making coupling, reflection and electromagnetic emissions more difficult to control. The numerical factor depends on the waveform definition and is not a universal law for every digital pulse.

PCB signal integrity: diagnosing reflections

The simulation study modeled a 10 cm microstrip trace on FR-4, with a nominal trace width of 1,000 μm, dielectric thickness of 1,600 μm, and relative permittivity of 4.8. Fast 3.3 V CMOS drivers excited the interconnect.

The original waveform showed ringing at the receiving end and an approximately 1 ns propagation delay. In the simulated emission spectrum, multiple peaks crossed the reference-limit curves displayed by the software.

Reflection coefficient at a load
ΓL = (ZL − Z0) / (ZL + Z0)

If the load impedance ZL differs from the line's characteristic impedance Z0, part of the traveling voltage wave is reflected. A suitable source-series resistor can reduce re-reflections by matching the driver output impedance plus series resistance to the trace impedance.

Series termination and slower drivers

A termination assistant recommended a 62.8 Ω series resistor near the driver. In the report's simulation, this eliminated the visible overshoot and ringing while retaining an approximately 1 ns propagation delay. The resulting emission spectrum also showed fewer prominent peaks relative to the software's reference curves.

Replacing the original fast CMOS driver with a 74HCT04 model produced a slower edge, approximately 7 ns rather than 1 ns, and improved the simulated received waveform without an additional series resistor in that configuration.

The report also explored IBIS (Input/Output Buffer Information Specification) behavioral models to account for driver and receiver behavior across typical, minimum and maximum conditions. The reported waveform analysis found rise times of approximately 7 ns at the source and 8 ns at the receiver.

Layer stackup, return paths and guard traces

The final investigations compared top-layer and internal-layer PCB routing. Moving a signal trace to an internal layer reduced several high-frequency components in the simulated emission spectrum. The study then modeled two neighboring traces and the voltage induced on an undriven victim net.

Adding a grounded guard trace between the two signal tracks reduced the induced voltage in the tested simulation. Removing that guard trace increased the disturbance. Routing the two signals on different internal layers also produced a slight reduction in coupling in the final configuration.

Engineering interpretation

The measured cable experiment and the simulated PCB examples lead to the same practical lesson: signal integrity and EMC depend on geometry, return paths, termination and edge rate. A correct logic level at the source does not guarantee a clean waveform at the receiver.

Scope and limitations

The ribbon-cable propagation and crosstalk observations were experimental; the PCB ringing, emissions and routing comparisons were simulation results. The displayed emission-limit curves are software references, not evidence of certified EMC compliance. Actual compliance would require measurements using the applicable standard and test setup. Similarly, the effectiveness of a guard trace depends on its grounding, placement and surrounding stackup.
